purpose: Carbamazepine is used to control certain types of seizures in people with epilepsy. It is also used to treat sharp, stabbing nerve pain in the face called trigeminal neuralgia. In some cases, doctors prescribe it to help stabilize mood in people with bipolar disorder.
how_it_works: Your brain and nerves communicate using tiny electrical signals. In conditions like epilepsy or nerve pain, these signals can become overactive and fire out of control. Carbamazepine works by calming those overactive signals, almost like a dimmer switch, so your nerves fire in a more normal, controlled way.
common_side_effects: Dizziness or feeling unsteady, drowsiness or tiredness, blurred or double vision, nausea or upset stomach, dry mouth, and headache. These side effects are often worse when you first start the medication and may improve over time.
warnings: This medication can rarely cause serious blood problems or a dangerous skin rash — call your doctor right away if you notice a rash, fever, sore throat, easy bruising, or unusual bleeding. It can also affect your liver, so regular blood tests are important. Carbamazepine interacts with many other medications, so always tell every doctor and pharmacist what you take. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can trigger seizures.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individual and your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it. A common starting dose for adults is 100 to 200 mg taken once or twice a day, gradually increased to 800 to 1200 mg per day in divided doses. Always take it exactly as prescribed and try to take it at the same times each day, with food to help reduce stomach upset.
